title: Event log record
description: One line of `.approval/log/events.jsonl` (SPEC.md §8). The log is append-only and is the truth; projections are caches. Every record MUST validate against this schema before append (SPEC.md §8: validation at the write boundary is itself a control). Structural shape only: hash-chain linkage, first-record semantics, and monotonic `seq` are verified by the chain verifier (M1), not expressible here.

seq.description: SPEC.md §8: 1-based position of this record in the append-only log. Strict monotonic succession across records is enforced by the chain verifier (M1); this schema constrains a single record only.

ts.description: SPEC.md §8: RFC 3339 timestamp at which the event was appended (the example record uses `2026-08-04T09:14:02Z`).

event.description: SPEC.md §8 'Event types (v0.1)': the closed set of eighteen event types. Closed by design — an unrecognized type fails closed at the write boundary rather than entering the log unvalidated. `payload.pruned` (APRV-38) is the first addition after the v0.1 draft set of sixteen and `approval.withdrawn` (APRV-106) the second: a reader of a v0.1 log may encounter either, and a verifier written against the draft enum must be updated to accept both.

actor.description: SPEC.md §8: who caused the event, as `<kind>:<id>` (the example record uses `human:carter`). Three kinds: `human:` for a person acting through a channel or the CLI, `agent:` for an agent-originated event, and `system:` for events the daemon originates with no external prompt (for example `approval.expired`, which fires on TTL lapse rather than on any actor's action). Approval decisions are restricted to `human:` — see the per-type rules below.

alg.description: SPEC.md §8 (hash-scheme amendment): explicit hash-scheme identifier. Version 0.1 defines exactly one value, `sha256/jcs` — SHA-256 over the RFC 8785 (JCS) canonical serialization of the record with `prev` included. Missing or unrecognized `alg` MUST be rejected; differing `alg` values MAY coexist in one log so a scheme change is a migration, never a schism.

hash.description: SPEC.md §8: this record's hash under `alg` — SHA-256 over the record's JCS canonical serialization with `prev` included, lowercase hex. That the digest actually matches the record contents is checked by `approval log verify` (M1); this schema constrains only its form.

prev.description: SPEC.md §8: the previous record's `hash`, chaining the log so that `approval log verify` detects any mutation or truncation. `null` is legal only for the first record in a log; a schema can express the type union but not the position, so first-record semantics are enforced by the chain verifier (M1).

task.description: SPEC.md §8: the Backlog.md task id the event concerns (the example record uses `task-042`). Optional in the base shape and required per event type below.

action_key.description: SPEC.md §8: the action's idempotency key (the example record uses `task-042:chaser:2026-08-04`), identifying the specific side effect being approved or executed. Optional in the base shape and required per event type below.

channel.description: SPEC.md §8: the channel through which the event reached the runtime (the example record uses `telegram`). Optional: CLI- and daemon-originated events need not name one.

payload.description: SPEC.md §8: event-type-specific detail (the example record carries an approver's note). Shape is deliberately open at v0.1; per-type payload schemas are a later, separate task.

allOf.$comment: SPEC.md §8: approval lifecycle events name both the task and the specific action being decided.

SPEC.md §10.1: granting and rejecting are human decisions made through the CLI or a channel. An agent- or system-originated grant would be the gate approving itself, so the actor MUST carry the `human:` prefix.

SPEC.md §5.2/§8 (APRV-56): reviewing a sampled action is a human decision, made through the CLI, and the runtime already refuses any other reviewer. A `system:` or `agent:` reviewer would be the party under oversight signing off on its own sample, which is the one reading of the record that must never be possible, so the actor MUST carry the `human:` prefix.

SPEC.md §6.3/§8 (APRV-106): a withdrawal is the requester retracting their own pending request, so the actor is the party that opened it — `agent:` for an agent-originated request, `human:` for a person's. Never `system:`: the runtime already has a way to end a request it was not asked to end, and that is `approval.expired` on TTL lapse. A `system:` withdrawal would let the runtime cancel a question a human was about to answer, with no clock to justify it. That the actor is the SAME party that appended the matching `approval.requested` is not expressible here (a schema sees one record), and is enforced by the gate as `not-requester`; what the schema can rule out is the actor kind that must never appear. `reason` is required and closed: a withdrawal that does not say why is a decision nobody can audit, and the three values are the three things that actually happen — the requester's wait elapsed, the requester changed its mind, or a newer request replaced this one.

actor.description: SPEC.md §6.3: the requester. `system:` is refused — expiry, not withdrawal, is the runtime's way to end a request.

action_key.description: The withdrawn request's idempotency key, restated in the payload so the reason and the key it applies to travel together for a reader who has only the payload.

reason.description: Why the requester retracted. `timeout`: the requester stopped waiting and can no longer consume a decision. `cancelled`: the requester no longer wants the action. `superseded`: a newer request covers the same effect.

note.description: The requester's free-text elaboration. Claimed, never a control.

allOf.$comment: SPEC.md §8: execution events report on one keyed action of one task.

SPEC.md §10.3 (amended, APRV-38): a decision collected as part of a batch gesture carries the batch's channel delivery id as a first-class payload field. Optional — a unit decision has no batch — and constrained only when present, so the field can never arrive as an empty string or a number that audit would have to guess at.

batch_delivery_id.description: SPEC.md §10.3: the channel delivery id of the batch this decision answered. The log never batches — each member gets its own event — so this field is what ties the separate events back to the one human gesture. Earlier v0.1 builds encoded the same id in the first line of `note` (`batch_delivery_id=<id>`); readers accept both encodings through v0.1 and prefer this one.

allOf.$comment: SPEC.md §8/§9 (amended, APRV-38): `payload.pruned` records that the daemon removed a payload file from `.approval/payloads/` under `payload_retention`. Two constraints, both about who and what: the actor is `system:` because pruning is a retention rule executing on a schedule rather than anyone's decision (a `human:` or `agent:` pruner would be a party under oversight deleting the evidence its approval bound to), and the payload names the removed bytes by their SHA-256, which is the store's own key and the same value a grant binds to. The log therefore states exactly what the store no longer holds.

payload_hash.description: SPEC.md §6.2/§9: SHA-256 (lowercase hex) of the pruned payload's bytes — the content address `.approval/payloads/` filed them under, and the value the action's grant bound to.

allOf.$comment: SPEC.md §8: task-scoped events that precede or accompany a specific action key. Budget accounting is per task (SPEC.md §5), so `budget.exceeded` names the task but need not name an action.
